summary:
Aruba is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands with its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, which governs discrimination and sexual offences on the island. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

The protection gap that matters most to a trans visitor is written into that code. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference with the purpose or effect of impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental freedoms in political, economic, social or cultural life or in other areas of public life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 attach penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds stop at sexual orientation; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. Aruba consequently offers a trans visitor no statutory ground of protection against discrimination and no discrimination offence based on gender identity that could be prosecuted.

Partner recognition runs through two channels. Registered unions open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples were adopted by the legislature on 8 September 2016 by 11 votes to 5 with four abstentions, after a campaign of two and a half years sponsored by the openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes, who publicly introduced the bill in August 2016, and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extended the marriage articles of the civil code to those unions and conferred spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights; Aruba's own news service reported the vote as the first such action by an island in the Caribbean. Under the ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands of 12 July 2024, same-sex marriage is legal in Aruba, and Aruba has been required since the ruling of 13 April 2007 to recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

The route by which couples in fact secured recognition was registration elsewhere in the Kingdom: marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom before the 2024 ruling, and the sponsor of the 2016 amendment had used exactly that route. For a trans visitor in a relationship that Aruban civil-code categories would read as same-sex, recognition turns on recorded legal sex. Religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao permitted such unions at the time.

Official signals are mixed. On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten, and Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered. In the opposite direction, the Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during the 2004 to 2007 court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

Violence tied to that challenge is documented rather than statistical: Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during the 2004 to 2007 proceedings, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. No trans-specific violence figures for Aruba and no general homicide rate appear in the sources, so no comparison of magnitude can be made.

Independent description of daily life is more qualified than the destination's promotion. GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud population than Curaçao, records that same-sex adoption is legal, and identifies Catholic influence as the main brake; it notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands. Gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad alongside venues, hotels and restaurants that cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly, and several associations are active, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and the Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted as saying: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

The Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, placing feeling safe, secure and welcome at the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. That is the destination's own marketer speaking rather than independent evidence, and it speaks to sexual orientation rather than gender identity; it nonetheless documents the mainstream positioning a visitor will encounter.
tangentialFactors:
The sharpest tension in the record is between Aruba's tourism positioning and its statute: the island markets itself to LGBT travellers as safe, secure and welcome while its only anti-discrimination ground is sexual orientation, leaving gender identity outside the code entirely.

Regional comparison: at the time of the 2016 registered-union amendment neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao permitted such unions, and Aruba's own news service reported the vote as the first of its kind on a Caribbean island. GlobalGayz describes Aruba's out-and-proud population as smaller and quieter than Curaçao's.

The 2015 endorsement of equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons was issued by all Kingdom governments, Aruba among them, but it is a political commitment rather than Aruban legislation and did not produce a gender-identity ground in the Aruban Criminal Code.
localsOnly:
Residents' formal rights: registered unions extend the marriage articles of the civil code and carry spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights, and same-sex adoption is legal. Same-sex marriage is legal in Aruba following the ruling of 12 July 2024, and marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba must be recognised.

Residents' protection gap: Articles 2:61 and 2:62 of the Aruban Criminal Code penalise discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds of sexual orientation with penalties from fines to one year of imprisonment, and gender identity is not an enumerated ground. A resident refused service, dismissed or harassed because of gender identity or gender expression has no ground of protection under Article 1:221.

Social environment: Aruba's own representation acknowledged at the 2015 Kingdom endorsement that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream opposition to LGBT rights. The Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba summarises the prevailing norm as acceptance as long as it is not in their face: people are out, but discreetly out.

Community infrastructure: gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and the Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba are active, and Igualdad Aruba's petition of nearly 20,000 signatures supported the 2016 registered-union amendment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No consulted source states how gender markers are changed on Aruban identity documents or civil-registry records, how a trans traveller's documents are handled at entry, or what screening practice applies at Aruba's ports. These points are unresolved.

The anti-discrimination provisions cited enumerate sexual orientation only; whether any other Aruban instrument reaches gender identity or gender expression is not sourced.

No enforcement data accompany Articles 2:61 and 2:62: the sources carry no prosecution counts, hate-crime statistics or complaints data. No trans-specific violence figures for Aruba and no general homicide rate appear, so no comparison of magnitude can be made.

Facilities law covering access to toilets, changing rooms and other single-sex spaces in Aruba is not addressed by any source. Marriage recognition depends on the legal sex classification of spouses, and no source states how Aruban civil authorities classify a trans spouse's recorded sex for the purpose of reading a marriage as same-sex. No findings are available on education, schooling, or minors' access to services or documentation.
